💬 Iran ready to help resolve Saudi-Yemen issues: Baqaei

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei says Iran is well-prepared to help resolve issues between Saudi Arabia and Yemen through peaceful means, stressing that the Islamic Republic remains steadfast in its principled position on the Yemen issue.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Baqaei outlined Iran’s position on the Saudi-Yemen conflict, calling for dialogue between the two sides to resolve their differences through diplomacy.
​
The spokesperson said Iran has always been ready to leverage its good offices to help end the conflict and remains prepared to use all its capabilities for this purpose if requested by the two sides.
​
Referring to the history of the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baqaei said developments over the past 12 years have shown that foreign intervention, a military approach and the blockade are not solutions to the Yemen crisis.
​
The official noted that the Yemeni people have endured the country’s air and sea blockade for more than a decade, showing remarkable patience in facing the consequences of an unjust blockade designed by actors from outside the region, particularly Britain and the United States.
​
Baqaei added that regional countries and the Muslim world are expected to make serious efforts to bring an end to the situation.
​
Commenting on a claim by a Saudi Foreign Ministry official that Iran had encouraged Yemenis to attack Saudi Arabia, the spokesperson rejected any alleged Iranian role in Yemeni operations.
​
Baqaei further stressed that Yemen’s armed forces act based on their own interests and assessments, saying such claims are not credible to those familiar with Iran’s relations with its allies and friends.
​
Iran does not consider an escalation of tensions to be in the interest of any side, he added.

🔻 Iran says all-front ceasefire essential to ending regional war

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh says ending the war on all fronts is a key condition for peace, stressing that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war persists across the region.

In an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, Khatibzadeh – who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials – said Iran remained committed to ending the Israeli war on Lebanon and had secured this objective in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which Iran and the United States signed in mid-June this year.
​
He said Lebanon was among the key issues discussed between Iran and the US, adding that he sought to bring the two sides closer during his visit to Beirut. Khatibzadeh said that he held “good” talks with Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and officials at the Foreign Ministry.
​
The Iranian official stressed that Israel must end its war in Lebanon and the Levant, noting that developments in both regions are interconnected.
​
One of Iran’s conditions is an end to all wars, he said, adding that if fighting continues on any one of these fronts, it means the war continues on all fronts. That is why Iran remained committed to ending the war in Lebanon and managed to achieve that goal, he noted.
​
The Iranian diplomat also said that Washington and Tel Aviv violated the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon, adding that US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached a deadlock. He said Israel could not be trusted to honor its commitments and that Washington was responsible for restraining its regional ally.
​
Khatibzadeh described the US war against Iran as illegal under international law, saying Washington had failed to destroy Iran’s air defenses and deterrence capabilities. He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
​
He added that Tehran was ready to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States over Iran’s peaceful nuclear activities, citing more than 15 IAEA reports that he said confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments.
​
Khatibzadeh also said Iran had proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, emphasizing that Tehran did not seek war but would resist any imposed conflict.
​
He further described Hezbollah as a Lebanese political party established to end Israeli attacks and occupation, adding that Iran’s relations with its allies were based on shared beliefs, values and principles.

MAY 18: The G7 conducts a coordinated exercise simulating a massive cross-border cyberattack affecting the financial sectors of all seven countries. Finance ministries, central banks, and financial regulators participate.

SEPTEMBER: British financial regulators warn that advanced AI is discovering cybersecurity vulnerabilities faster than some financial institutions can address them.

OCTOBER 6: South Korea reports suspected AI-assisted cyberattacks against commercial banks.

OCTOBER 8: The Bank of England, UK Treasury, regulators, and 38 major financial institutions conduct SIMEX26, simulating a global cloud-services disruption capable of affecting financial markets.

OCTOBER 13: Reuters reports that the Federal Reserve and other banking regulators are intensifying scrutiny of AI-related cybersecurity threats and banks’ dependence on third-party technology providers.

OCTOBER 14: The heads of the IMF and Bank of England warn that major cyberattacks could undermine public confidence in financial institutions and potentially threaten financial stability.

OCTOBER 15: Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden discusses preparing banks to rebuild compromised systems following catastrophic cyberattacks, alongside emerging quantum-computing threats to encryption.

OCTOBER 16: G7 finance ministers agree to prepare coordinated exercises simulating AI-enhanced cyberattacks against banks and critical financial infrastructure.

Think about the progression here.

We’ve gone from warnings about foreign adversaries infiltrating American infrastructure, to governments conducting international cyberattack simulations, to central banks openly discussing scenarios involving catastrophic financial disruptions.

And now the G7 is preparing for AI-driven attacks against the banking system.

But perhaps the most important development is the growing emphasis on PUBLIC CONFIDENCE.

Financial authorities are acknowledging that a major cyberattack wouldn’t necessarily have to destroy the banking system to create a crisis.

It could simply undermine public confidence in the system’s ability to function.

And THAT is where this becomes particularly interesting in the context of the broader financial restructuring narrative we’ve been following.

We’ve spent months examining the Trump administration’s moves involving sovereign wealth, strategic assets, gold, digital currencies, and potential alternatives to the legacy central banking structure.

Now, simultaneously, the world’s most powerful financial institutions are publicly preparing for scenarios that could threaten confidence in that very system.

The convergence of these developments deserves serious attention.
